selection.rule: Dependency-complete first 24 questions from the question-sheet selection order.

questions.question: What are the two main ideas named in this passage as the First Truth?
questions.answer: They are createdness and contingency.

questions.question: Which groups of Muslim thinkers are said to have supported these two ideas with many proofs?
questions.answer: Scholars of Islamic belief and theology, along with Muslim sages.

questions.question: What observation about the world leads them to say the world is not eternal?
questions.answer: They see that things in the world keep changing and shifting.

questions.question: According to the passage, what follows if the world is created?
questions.answer: It must have a Maker.

questions.question: What does the passage say about a thing whose own essence does not require either its existence or its nonexistence?
questions.answer: Its existence is only possible, not necessary, so it is not eternal.

questions.question: Why does the passage connect contingency with the need for a Creator?
questions.answer: If things do not exist by necessity in themselves, then their existence must come from One who gives it to them.

questions.question: What is the main conclusion of the whole passage?
questions.answer: The changing and dependent world points to the existence of a Maker who is not created or dependent.

questions.question: According to the passage, can a contingent thing be eternal by its own nature?
questions.answer: No, because it does not have existence from itself.

questions.question: Give a short summary of the passage in one sentence.
questions.answer: Because the world changes and does not exist by itself, it must have been created by a Maker.

questions.question: What is being introduced by the heading “First Truth”?
questions.answer: A proof based on createdness and contingency.

questions.question: How does the passage describe the amount of evidence for this proof?
questions.answer: It says the evidence is countless.

questions.question: What feature of the world is directly noticed first in the argument?
questions.answer: The world shows ongoing change.

questions.question: Why does ongoing change matter in this argument?
questions.answer: Because it shows the world does not stay the same forever and so is not eternal in itself.

questions.question: What conclusion is drawn after saying the world is created?
questions.answer: That there is a Creator who made it.

questions.question: What does contingency mean here in simple words?
questions.answer: It means a thing could exist or not exist; its existence is not required by itself.

questions.question: If existence and nonexistence are equally possible for something, what does that say about it?
questions.answer: It is not necessary by itself.

questions.question: What cause-and-effect chain appears in the passage from change to belief in a Maker?
questions.answer: Change shows the world is not eternal; if it is created, it needs a Creator.

questions.question: What is one central lesson from the whole passage?
questions.answer: The world’s changing and dependent nature points to a Maker beyond it.

questions.question: What claim do Muslim theologians and sages make about the world in this passage?
questions.answer: They say the world is created and not uncreated.

questions.question: What evidence from everyday reality do they start with?
questions.answer: They start with the fact that things change.

questions.question: What does the passage say cannot be true about a changing world?
questions.answer: That it is uncreated and eternal in itself.

questions.question: What must exist if the world was brought into existence?
questions.answer: A Maker must exist.

questions.question: What does the passage teach about the inner nature of contingent things?
questions.answer: Their own nature does not make their existence necessary.

questions.question: If a thing could just as well not exist, what category does it belong to in this argument?
questions.answer: It belongs to the category of contingent things.
